reference.source: Cummings Otolaryngology - Head and Neck Surgery
clinicalPearls: A congenital lateral neck lesion arising from incomplete involution of the embryonic branchial apparatus, most commonly the second cleft
Typically presents as a painless, fluctuant swelling along the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid, often becoming apparent in late childhood or young adulthood
Second-cleft anomalies characteristically lie in the upper lateral neck, whereas first-cleft lesions relate to the ear and parotid region
The lesion may enlarge or become tender during or after an upper respiratory tract infection
A cyst without an external opening is common, but associated sinuses or fistulae may discharge onto the skin
Ultrasound and cross-sectional imaging define the lesion and its relationship to the carotid sheath, and help plan surgery
A new cystic lateral neck mass in an adult over about forty must not be assumed benign, as cystic metastasis from HPV-related oropharyngeal carcinoma can mimic it
Definitive treatment is complete surgical excision of the cyst and any associated tract to prevent recurrence
reference.pathophysiology: Branchial cleft anomalies result from failure of the branchial (pharyngeal) apparatus to fully regress during embryonic development. Persistent epithelial remnants of a cleft or pouch give rise to cysts, sinuses or fistulae in characteristic locations determined by the arch of origin. The second branchial cleft accounts for the majority; its tract, when complete, passes from the tonsillar fossa between the internal and external carotid arteries to the lower lateral neck. Cysts are lined by squamous or respiratory epithelium, often with associated lymphoid tissue, and can enlarge or become infected, particularly after upper respiratory infections.
additionalDifferentials: Cystic metastatic squamous cell carcinoma, especially HPV-related
Thyroglossal duct cyst when close to the midline
Carotid body tumour or other neurogenic mass
additionalInvestigations: Ultrasound of the neck to characterise the cystic lesion
Contrast-enhanced CT or MRI to define extent and relationship to the carotid sheath
Fine-needle aspiration cytology, with careful interpretation given overlap with cystic metastasis
Panendoscopy and evaluation of the oropharynx in adults to exclude an occult primary tumour
HPV or p16 testing on aspirate or tissue when malignancy is a concern
redFlags: New cystic lateral neck mass in an adult, raising suspicion of metastatic carcinoma
Rapid growth, fixation, or associated mucosal lesion
Recurrent infection with abscess formation and airway or swallowing compromise
Associated cranial nerve deficits suggesting a more sinister process
reference.prognosis: For a true congenital branchial cyst, complete excision is generally curative with low recurrence, though incomplete removal of an associated tract predisposes to recurrence. The main clinical hazard is misclassifying a malignant cystic metastasis as a benign branchial cyst, which delays cancer treatment.
pitfalls: Assuming a cystic neck mass in an older adult is benign without excluding metastatic carcinoma
Incomplete excision of the tract leading to recurrence or a persistent fistula
Repeated drainage of an infected cyst without definitive excision
Injuring adjacent structures such as the great vessels or cranial nerves during dissection
references: Cummings Otolaryngology - Head and Neck Surgery
Scott-Brown's Otorhinolaryngology, Head and Neck Surgery
management: Complete surgical excision of the cyst together with any associated sinus or fistulous tract for definitive cure
Control of active infection with antibiotics and drainage before undertaking elective excision
Cross-sectional imaging to define the tract and its relationship to the carotid sheath for surgical planning
Exclusion of a cystic nodal metastasis in adults through panendoscopy and HPV or p16 testing before assuming a benign lesion
Meticulous complete removal of the tract to minimise recurrence
Referral to otolaryngology or head and neck surgery
